title: They Saw a Game
text:
On November 23, 1951, Princeton played Dartmouth in the last football game of the season. It was a rough game. Princeton's star player, Dick Kazmaier, left with a broken nose in the second quarter, and a Dartmouth player later left with a broken leg. Penalties piled up on both sides. Afterward the student newspapers of both colleges gave very different accounts of who was to blame.

The psychologists Albert Hastorf of Dartmouth and Hadley Cantril of Princeton saw an opportunity. They asked students at both universities questions about the game, and showed a film of it to groups of students from each school. While watching, each student marked every rule violation they saw, and whether it was flagrant or mild.

The two groups seemed to have watched different games. Princeton students saw the Dartmouth team commit more than twice as many infractions as their own team. Dartmouth students saw the two sides commit about equal numbers. Most Princeton students thought the game was rough and dirty and that Dartmouth had started it; many Dartmouth students thought it was rough but fair.

Hastorf and Cantril concluded that there was no single game that people simply observed. Each person selected and interpreted what they saw according to what mattered to them.
lesson: Loyalties shape what we literally see, not only how we judge it. When you disagree about the facts with someone on the other side, assume both views are colored.
location: Princeton University and Dartmouth College, USA
source: Hastorf, A. H., and Cantril, H. (1954). They saw a game: A case study. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 49(1), 129-134.
